title: High Tight Flag
teaches: The high tight flag as we trade it: a quiet, liquid leader nearly doubles in a few weeks on a real change, pauses a few weeks a little under the high on lighter volume with tight closes, the buy is the trade through the pattern high at market, the stop sits a few cents under the day's low, a third comes off at 3R and 5R with the rest on the trail, and a loss at the stop is the system working.

facts.quote: First, a stock must gain 100% to 120% in a span of four to eight weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: first, the stock gains 100% to 120% in four to eight weeks.

facts.quote: The second element, the flag itself, forms as the stock pulls back, usually 10% to 20% or sometimes 25%, in the next three to five weeks.
facts.claim: IBD: the flag pulls back usually 10% to 20%, sometimes 25%, over the next three to five weeks.

facts.quote: Similar to the handle portion for a cup-with-handle base, volume generally dries up. Big fund managers are holding the stock.
facts.claim: IBD: volume generally dries up in the flag.

facts.quote: Element number three is the breakout, when the stock clears the peak of the flagpole in big turnover, meaning daily volume that's at least 40% above average.
facts.claim: IBD: the breakout clears the peak of the flagpole, on volume at least 40% above average.

facts.quote: High, tight flags are high-risk bases. Many fail.

facts.quote: Weekly trading ranges were a little wild and wooly, but the closes were relatively tight.
facts.claim: IBD on JDSU: wide weekly ranges, but relatively tight closes.

facts.quote: But the action appears tight vs. the steep run-up before the base.
facts.claim: IBD: the flag looks tight next to the steep run-up before it.

facts.quote: the stock showed a 98 Composite Rating as well as 81 EPS and 98 RS grades.
facts.claim: IBD: Taser showed a 98 RS grade at its breakout.

facts.quote: If you're lucky, you'll spot one or two of those in a bull market.
facts.claim: IBD (quoted by Bonde): if you are lucky, one or two in a bull market.

facts.quote: The stock triggered the 8% sell rule two weeks after the breakout but regained the buy point the same week
facts.claim: IBD: Taser triggered IBD's 8% sell rule after the breakout, then regained the buy point.

facts.quote: One needs to take the earnings rate and whether it is first base.

facts.claim: Bulkowski: flags with a down-sloping top tend to outperform.

walkthroughs.title: SRPT, June 2015: the textbook pole and flag
steps: SRPT, 2015. A report, then a +60% day tops a near-vertical two-week run: +129% in 14 sessions.
Then a 14-day sideways flag, 15.0% deep, on lighter volume. It holds the 21-day EMA. The pattern high is the line.
2015-06-10: it trades through the high. Buy at market, 27.50. Stop a few cents under the day's low, 26.59.
Failure mode: a breakout nobody buys, stopped next session. Instead 3R comes on day 5. Trim a third, stop to breakeven.

walkthroughs.title: SOFI, November 2024: a gap over the high
steps: SOFI, 2024. The pole holds a report: +91% in 28 sessions. Then a 7-day flag, 9.9% deep.
The pattern high is 14.44. The stock gaps over it. The open is 1.5% past the high, inside the 4% line.
So the fill is the open, 14.65, at market. The stop sits under the day's low, 14.24: 2.8% of risk.
Failure mode: a close back under the high, stop taken next day. Instead 3R comes on day 3.

walkthroughs.title: BIDU, February 2021: trims, then the trail
steps: BIDU, 2021. A large-cap double, +100% in 36 sessions. A 12-day flag, 13.2% deep, on lighter volume.
2021-02-05: buy at market as it clears the high, 264.95. Stop under the day's low, 255.06.
3R on day 2: a third off, stop to breakeven. Another third at 5R. It runs to about 354.
Failure mode: it unwinds as fast as it rose. Under the flag low by late March. The trail got you out.

questions.q: In one line, what is a high tight flag?
choices: A short rest after a near-double
A long box after a modest run up
Pullbacks that shrink for months
A sharp rebound off a crash low
questions.answer: A short rest after a near-double
questions.why: A short pause after a near-double. IBD: first the stock gains 100% to 120% in four to eight weeks. Then the flag forms as it pulls back.
questions.lesson_line: A high tight flag is a rocket catching its breath for a few weeks, a little under the high.

wrong.A long box after a modest run up: That is a flat base. The flag follows a far bigger, faster run and rests for weeks, not months.
wrong.Pullbacks that shrink for months: That is a VCP. The flag is one shelf a little under the high of the pole.
wrong.A sharp rebound off a crash low: That is a V. Bulkowski says to avoid V shapes, where price drops hard into the start of the pole.

questions.q: On a high tight flag the stop goes at the flag's low.
questions.why: False. The flag low is the line that kills the idea, not the stop. The stop sits a few cents under the entry day's low or the prior day's low.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low kills the idea. The day's low is the stop.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: We buy at market as price trades above the peak of the ___, never on a trendline inside the flag.
questions.why: The pole. IBD: the breakout clears the peak of the flagpole. Bulkowski: buy above the highest high in the pattern, not a trendline break.
questions.lesson_line: The buy is above the top of the whole pattern, usually the pole's peak.

questions.q: In a proper flag, volume runs heavier than it did on the pole.
questions.why: False. Flag volume runs below the pole's average. IBD: volume generally dries up. Bulkowski: it recedes for best performance.
questions.lesson_line: Loud on the way up, quiet in the flag. Holders are not selling.

questions.q: Where does the best pole usually start?
choices: A quiet base, then real news
A crash low, still falling hard
The third leg of a long run
Under a falling 200-day average
questions.answer: A quiet base, then real news
questions.why: A quiet base, then real news. Kuhn: a long, well-contained base first, then a news event lifts the stock. Bulkowski: poles springing from flat bases work better.
questions.lesson_line: A sleeper that wakes up on news is the start you want, not a crash bounce.

wrong.A crash low, still falling hard: That is the V Bulkowski says to avoid. A rebound off a crash is not a fresh pole.
wrong.The third leg of a long run: Late legs break down. Bonde: a tight flag late in the move breaks down.
wrong.Under a falling 200-day average: We do not buy under the 200-day. A real pole starts from a base, not a downtrend.

questions.q: Bulkowski says a high tight flag often does not look like a flag at all.
questions.why: True. It is just a pause in the price rise. IBD: the action looks tight next to the steep run-up before it.
questions.lesson_line: Do not hunt for a neat flag shape. Look for a pause that holds near the high.

questions.q: IBD says how many of these you might find in a whole bull market?
choices: One or two, with some luck
About one every single week
A dozen or so every month
Hundreds in each daily scan
questions.answer: One or two, with some luck
questions.why: One or two, if you are lucky. Bonde: if you find too many high tight flags, your reading is wrong. Our scan found only 12 liquid hits in 36 years before 2020.
questions.lesson_line: If you see one every week, you are calling ordinary flags by the wrong name.

wrong.About one every single week: Far too many. It is rare, and Bonde warns that seeing too many means a misreading.
wrong.A dozen or so every month: That many means ordinary tight flags are being called by this name.
wrong.Hundreds in each daily scan: A scan that returns hundreds is catching bull flags, not near-doubles.

questions.q: A 30% run followed by a very tight flag counts as a high tight flag.
questions.why: False. Measure the pole. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight.
questions.lesson_line: The pole names the setup. Tightness alone never does.

questions.q: How do we measure the flag's depth?
choices: Pattern high to flag low, on price
As a share of the pole's height
From the first close to the last
From the 200-day to the low
questions.answer: Pattern high to flag low, on price
questions.why: On price, from the pattern's highest high to the flag's lowest low, divided by the high. Kuhn measures on the advance instead, which gives a bigger number for the same flag.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low on price. Measure it; do not eyeball it.

wrong.As a share of the pole's height: That is Kuhn's way, on the advance. For the same flag it gives a bigger number, so it rejects flags IBD accepts.
wrong.From the first close to the last: That is drift, not depth. Depth runs from the highest high to the lowest low.
wrong.From the 200-day to the low: The 200-day is a context line, not part of the flag.

questions.q: Do the closes pass our tightness test?
questions.story: A stock doubled in five weeks after an earnings beat. It now pauses nine sessions under the high. Daily ranges are wide, but the last five closes sit 4% apart.
choices: Yes, within 10% of each other
No, the daily ranges are too wide
No, they must sit within 1%
questions.why: Yes. In the last 5 sessions before the trigger, the highest close is no more than 10% above the lowest. These sit 4% apart.
questions.lesson_line: Test the closes, not the wicks. Wild ranges with tight closes still count.

wrong.No, the daily ranges are too wide: The test is on closes. IBD on JDSU: wild weekly ranges, but the closes were tight.
wrong.No, they must sit within 1%: Our line is 10%. A pause that tight is rare and not required.

questions.q: Before the entry, a close below the flag's low ends the setup.
questions.why: True. A close below the flag's low before entry ends it. The flag low is the line that kills the idea.
questions.lesson_line: Under the flag low, the idea is dead. Wait for a new setup.

questions.q: Which flag top grades best?
choices: Flat or sloping down
Rising, higher highs each day
Loose and jagged
A sharp V back to the pole low
questions.why: Flat or sloping down. Bulkowski: flags with a down-sloping top tend to outperform. TraderLion says the same, with no statistic.
questions.lesson_line: A flag that leans back against the run is holders resting, not buyers chasing.

wrong.Rising, higher highs each day: Higher highs through the pause is buyers chasing. The A+ shape is flat or down.
wrong.Loose and jagged: Bulkowski: trade tight flags, not loose ones.
wrong.A sharp V back to the pole low: Falling back to the pole low gives back the whole run. That is no flag.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A trade still under 1R after ___ trading days is sold.
questions.why: 10. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
questions.lesson_line: Give it two weeks to pay. Under 1R by then, it goes.

questions.q: Once you are filled, a real stop order goes in with the broker straight away.
questions.why: True. A real stop order with the broker, not one kept in your head. It only moves up.
questions.lesson_line: Filled, then stop in. Same minute.

questions.q: What flag volume makes the A grade on our card?
choices: 60% of the pole's or less
Above the pole's average
Exactly the pole's average
Twice the pole's average
questions.why: 60% of the pole's or less is the A grade. Any flag volume below the pole's passes the gate; the lighter, the better.
questions.lesson_line: Quieter flag, better grade. Under the pole's volume is the floor.

wrong.Above the pole's average: That ends the setup: supply is coming in, not drying up.
wrong.Exactly the pole's average: The gate is below the pole's. Equal is not drying up.
wrong.Twice the pole's average: Heavy volume in the rest is selling. That is the opposite of the A grade.

questions.q: Which stop is ours on a high tight flag?
choices: A few cents under the day's low
At the very bottom of the flag
A flat 8% under the buy price
Half the pole under the high
questions.answer: A few cents under the day's low
questions.why: A few cents under the day's low. A few cents under the entry day's low, or the prior day's low. The size comes from that stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, a few cents under the day's low. Then the size.

wrong.At the very bottom of the flag: That is Bulkowski's stop. For us the flag low kills the idea; it is not the stop.
wrong.A flat 8% under the buy price: That is IBD's general sell rule, not a stop for this base. Taser triggered it and then recovered.
wrong.Half the pole under the high: That is far too wide. Our stop usually sits within about 3% of the buy.

questions.q: You are in, and the breakout day ends on light volume. That alone is a reason to sell before the stop.
questions.why: False. Light breakout volume is not a reason to exit. After the entry, the stop is the exit, with the time stop and the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Once you are in, the stop decides. Not the volume bar.

questions.q: Bulkowski's measure rule adds half the pole to the flag low. What is it for us?
choices: A reference, not a sell rule
Our target; sell it all there
Where the stop goes
Where the first third goes
questions.answer: A reference, not a sell rule
questions.why: A reference, not a sell rule. We have no price target: a third at 3R, another third at 5R, then trail the rest.
questions.lesson_line: We sell by R and by the trail, never by a projected target.

wrong.Our target; sell it all there: We have no price target. The trims are in R and the rest rides the trail.
wrong.Where the stop goes: The stop is a few cents under the day's low, not a projection.
wrong.Where the first third goes: The first third comes off at 3R, measured from your fill and stop.

questions.q: On a high tight flag our hard rule sells the first third at 5R.
questions.why: False. The hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R. Ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R; in practice we mostly wait for 5R.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R is the hard rule. Know the price before the open.

questions.q: Bought at 27.50 with the stop at 26.59. Where is 3R?
questions.why: 30.23. One R is the fill minus the stop. Add three of those to the fill. SRPT got there on day 5.
questions.lesson_line: Know your 3R before the open. The first third comes off there.

questions.q: What usually sits behind the pole?
choices: A real business change or news
Nothing at all; poles are random
A stock split or a name change
A big index fund rebalance
questions.answer: A real business change or news
questions.why: A real change, like an earnings beat. With heavy volume it is the A+ context. Seven of the ten examples had a report inside the pole.
questions.lesson_line: Ask why it doubled. A real change in the business is the best answer.

wrong.Nothing at all; poles are random: Kuhn: an important news event usually lifts the stock out of dormancy.
wrong.A stock split or a name change: A split changes the share count, not the business. It is no reason to double.
wrong.A big index fund rebalance: Flows can move a stock, but the card's A+ context is a change in the business.

questions.q: At the trigger, the close must be above the 200-day average.
questions.why: True. The close is above the 200-day at the trigger. No longs below the 200-day is a hard rule.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day, always. Most of these are far above it.

questions.q: The lowest low of the 40 sessions was 12.40 and the pole high is 26.00. How big is the pole, in percent?
questions.why: 109.7%. The pole high over the low, minus one. IBD looks for 100% to 120%; Bulkowski for at least 90%. This one more than doubled.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the pole before you look at the flag.

questions.q: Pattern high 100.00, flag low 84.00. How deep is the flag, in percent?
questions.why: 16%. The pattern high minus the flag low, divided by the high. IBD's flag usually pulls back 10% to 20%.
questions.lesson_line: Depth is high to low on price, divided by the high.

questions.q: Fill 14.65, stop 14.24. How far below the fill is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 2.8%. The fill minus the stop, divided by the fill. Inside the 3% the stop usually sits within. That was SOFI's stop.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.

questions.q: Bought at 264.95, stop 255.06. The stock trades to 314.40. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5R. The gain divided by the fill minus the stop. That is where the second third comes off; BIDU got there.
questions.lesson_line: Count in R, not dollars. 5R is the second trim.

questions.q: Account 100,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 132.97, stop 128.10. How many shares?
questions.why: 102. Account times risk percent, divided by the fill minus the stop, rounded down. The full size at one price and one stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size. Never the other way round.

questions.q: The 10-day average is 50.00. Above what price is a buy too stretched?
questions.why: 55.00. Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average. About 5% over it is the A+ zone.
questions.lesson_line: Read the stretch in percent before you read the pattern.

questions.q: Buy the open, or pass?
questions.story: The pattern high is 60.00 and your alert sits there. News hits overnight. The stock opens at 63.30.
choices: Pass; past the 4% line
Buy; the breakout is real
Buy half size
Buy with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. 63.30 is more than 4% over 60.00. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the shares shrink.
questions.lesson_line: I would rather miss it than chase it. Four percent and done.

wrong.Buy; the breakout is real: Real and too far away are both true. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.Buy half size: Half of a bad entry is still a bad entry.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: Widening the stop to fit a late entry is the mistake, not the fix.

questions.q: Buy the break today?
questions.story: The pole came off a report. The flag is 12 sessions old and tight. The next report is in 2 sessions.
choices: No; a report is too close
Yes; the flag is tight
Yes, at half size
Yes, and sell before the report
questions.answer: No; a report is too close
questions.why: No. No new buy in the 3 sessions before a report. These poles often follow a report, and the next one can land inside the flag.
questions.lesson_line: Check the report date every time. Inside 3 sessions, wait.

wrong.Yes; the flag is tight: A tight flag does not change the calendar. The window comes first.
wrong.Yes, at half size: The rule is no new buy, not a smaller one.
wrong.Yes, and sell before the report: The rule is no new buy inside the window, not a quick trip in and out.

questions.q: What is your stop now?
questions.story: Bought at 52.00, stop 51.00. Bad news overnight: it opens at 50.40. The first 30-minute bar's low is 50.10.
choices: The first 30-minute low
Sell at the open, no matter what
The flag's low
No stop until it recovers
questions.why: The first 30-minute low is the new stop. A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The loss at that low is inside the 2R ceiling.
questions.lesson_line: On a gap through the stop, let the first 30 minutes set the new stop.

wrong.Sell at the open, no matter what: Our gap rule lets the first 30 minutes decide, with a ceiling at 2R.
wrong.The flag's low: That widens the stop. The gap rule is the one exception, and it uses the 30-minute low.
wrong.No stop until it recovers: Every position has a real stop. A gap changes where it sits, not whether it exists.

questions.q: A wicky breakout bar that closes well off its high grades lower than a strong close.
questions.why: True. A strong close on the breakout day raises the grade; a wicky bar that closes off its high is B-.
questions.lesson_line: Where the breakout day closes tells you who won the day.

questions.q: Widen the stop, hold it, or sell?
questions.story: Four days after the breakout the stock drifts back to the pattern high. Your stop under the entry day's low has not been touched.
choices: Hold; the stop is the exit
Widen it to the flag low
Sell now, before it fails
Add more at the pattern high
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Two in three winners come back to the breakout price within a month.
questions.lesson_line: A test of the breakout is normal. The stop is the answer, not your nerves.

wrong.Widen it to the flag low: The stop never moves down. Widening it is the mistake the rule exists to stop.
wrong.Sell now, before it fails: A pullback to the breakout price is common. Selling early turns a normal test into a loss.
wrong.Add more at the pattern high: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.q: What does the time stop say?
questions.story: Ten trading days after the breakout, the trade is up 1.3R. It is grinding higher, not running.
choices: Keep it; it is over 1R
Sell; it has not reached 3R
Sell half now
Move the stop to the flag low
questions.why: Keep it. The time stop sells a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days. This one is over 1R. TMDX took 23 sessions to 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Slow is not wrong. Under 1R after ten days is the line.

wrong.Sell; it has not reached 3R: The time stop is 1R after ten days, not 3R.
wrong.Sell half now: No rule sells half here. The trims come at 3R and 5R.
wrong.Move the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. The flag low is below it.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
questions.story: Bought at 40.00, stop 39.00, so 3R is 43.00. The next morning it opens at 43.60.
choices: Sell one third at the open
Wait for a dip back to 43.00
Sell the whole lot at the open
Do nothing at all until 5R
questions.answer: Sell one third at the open
questions.why: Sell the first third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, take that trim at the open.
questions.lesson_line: A trim level the open jumps over is taken at the open, not waited for.

wrong.Wait for a dip back to 43.00: The open already passed 3R. Waiting for a dip can leave the trim untaken.
wrong.Sell the whole lot at the open: A third comes off at 3R. The rest keeps working.
wrong.Do nothing at all until 5R: The hard rule is a third at 3R. The open is past it.

questions.q: The first third is off at 3R. Where does the stop go?
choices: To breakeven, your fill
Leave it under the entry day
Down to the flag low
Up to the 3R price
questions.why: To breakeven. The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default.
questions.lesson_line: First trim, then breakeven. The rest of the trade is free.

wrong.Leave it under the entry day: At the first trim it moves up to breakeven by default.
wrong.Up to the 3R price: The default at the first trim is breakeven, not the trim price.

questions.q: This stock trades 3,000,000 shares a day. The most you would own?
choices: 30,000 shares, 1% of a day
300,000 shares
3,000 shares
No limit with a tight stop
questions.why: 30,000 shares. Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume. Thin, fast names limit size.
questions.lesson_line: One percent of the daily volume is the ceiling, however tight the stop.

wrong.300,000 shares: That is a tenth of the day's volume. You could not get out without moving it.
wrong.3,000 shares: That is a tenth of the ceiling. The line is 1%.
wrong.No limit with a tight stop: A tight stop cannot catch a gap. The ceiling stands.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: The stock doubled in six weeks and now flags tight. It trades at 8.40, about $35 million a day.
choices: Pass; it is under $10
Take it; the dollar volume is fine
Take it at half size
Take it with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. Only stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. Bonde: some hits are too low priced and need liquidity.
questions.lesson_line: Cheap and thin is not ours, however good the chart.

wrong.Take it; the dollar volume is fine: Both tests apply: $10 or more and $20 million a day. Price fails.
wrong.Take it at half size: The floor is a gate, not a size cue.
wrong.Take it with a wider stop: A wider stop does not fix a stock we do not trade.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: A clean flag sets up after a double. The market reading has been Red for two weeks. Most leaders are breaking down.
choices: Pass; Red is mostly cash
Buy full size; the chart is A+
Buy and widen the stop
Buy a starter, add later
questions.why: Pass. A Red reading is mostly cash and shorts. Bulkowski: if the market looks about to drop, avoid the trade.
questions.lesson_line: The market first, then the chart. A great flag in a Red market waits.

wrong.Buy full size; the chart is A+: Red is mostly cash. Even Orange takes only A+ setups, and this is Red.
wrong.Buy and widen the stop: A wider stop is never the answer, in any market.
wrong.Buy a starter, add later: We never add. And Red is not the time to start.

questions.q: What relative strength do we want on this setup?
choices: An RS rating of 80 or more
Anything over 50 is fine
RS does not matter on this one
Only a rating of 99 or better
questions.answer: An RS rating of 80 or more
questions.why: An RS rating of 80 or more, in one of the strongest groups. After a doubling it is almost automatic: Taser showed a 98 RS at its breakout.
questions.lesson_line: Buy leaders. A double usually makes one.

wrong.Anything over 50 is fine: Our floor is 80. Half the market sits above 50.
wrong.RS does not matter on this one: Buy leaders is our rule on every long setup except parabolic and mean-reversion trades.
wrong.Only a rating of 99 or better: Too narrow. The floor is 80, with 90 or more as the A+ cue.

questions.q: A VCP is one shelf a little under the high; a high tight flag strings shrinking pullbacks.
questions.why: False. The two are swapped. A VCP strings several contractions after an advance; this setup is one shelf under the high of a huge pole.
questions.lesson_line: Several shrinking dips is a VCP. One shelf after a rocket is the flag.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: The stock was up 250% in the six months before this pole began. Now it doubles again and pauses tight.
choices: Pass; too late in the move
A+, with more momentum
Buy it; tight is tight
A fresh first base off a low
questions.answer: Pass; too late in the move
questions.why: Pass. The gate is not late: no more than 200% up in the 6 months before the pole. This one was up 250%. Bonde: a tight flag late in the move breaks down.
questions.lesson_line: Early legs pay. A flag after a giant run is where tired moves end.

wrong.A+, with more momentum: Momentum this late is the risk, not the edge. The not-late line is a gate.
wrong.Buy it; tight is tight: Tightness does not fix a late flag. Bonde: late flags break down.
wrong.A fresh first base off a low: After 250% in six months it is not first. The count starts at the quiet base.

questions.q: Which entry did Bulkowski find fails too often on this pattern?
choices: A trendline break in the flag
A trade above the highest high
A buy at the next day's open
A close above the pole top
questions.answer: A trendline break in the flag
questions.why: A trendline break in the flag. Too many fail even after a trendline break. Buy above the highest high in the pattern instead.
questions.lesson_line: Never buy the line inside the flag. Buy the top of the pattern.

wrong.A trade above the highest high: That is the entry he recommends, and ours: through the pattern high.
wrong.A buy at the next day's open: That is a timing choice, not the entry he tested and rejected.
wrong.A close above the pole top: He uses a close above the top to confirm the pattern, not to reject it.

questions.q: Pole low 10.00, pole high 20.00, flag low 17.00. Where is Bulkowski's reference level?
questions.why: 22.00. Take half of the pole and add it to the bottom of the flag. A reference only; we sell by R and the trail.
questions.lesson_line: Know the level if you like. It is never the reason to sell.

questions.q: High tight flag or bull flag?
questions.story: The stock ran 45% in three weeks on strong earnings. It paused six sessions in a tight range near the high.
choices: A bull flag
A high tight flag
A flat base
questions.why: A bull flag. Measure the pole: this one never doubled. A tight flag that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight.
questions.lesson_line: Doubled and paused is the rare one. Ran and paused is the common flag.

wrong.A high tight flag: The run is less than half a double. The pole names the setup.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base rests for weeks in a box. This is a short drift right after a run.

questions.q: Which card do you grade it on?
questions.story: The stock doubled in seven weeks. Then it rested 38 sessions in a 9% box near the high.
choices: Flat base; the rest is too long
High tight flag; the price doubled
Bull flag; the box is tight
questions.answer: Flat base; the rest is too long
questions.why: The flat base. Count the rest. IBD's flag forms over the next three to five weeks, and 38 sessions is far past that.
questions.lesson_line: A flag is a few weeks. A rest of months is a different base, graded as that base.

wrong.High tight flag; the price doubled: The double fits, but the rest runs far past a few weeks. It has become a base.
wrong.Bull flag; the box is tight: A bull flag is a short drift after a smaller run. This is a long box.

questions.q: Buy the pause, or not?
questions.story: The pole's last three days gapped up each morning on rising volume. The climax day opened high and closed below its open. Now it pauses.
choices: Not; a possible parabolic top
Buy it; the pause is tight
Buy over the climax day's high
questions.why: Not. A burst into a climax day that closed below its open is a possible parabolic top, not a flag. Bulkowski prefers a pole of about 45 degrees.
questions.lesson_line: Read the last leg of the pole. A burst that reverses is a top, not a flag.

wrong.Buy it; the pause is tight: Tight does not cancel the reversal. The card calls it a possible top.
wrong.Buy over the climax day's high: The trigger is fine on a flag. This is not a flag.

questions.q: Which card fits?
questions.story: The stock rose 35% in six weeks. Then it tightened for four weeks with higher lows, riding its rising short averages.
choices: Qullamaggie breakout
High tight flag setup
A V off a crash low
questions.why: The Qullamaggie breakout. It needs only a 30% move in the past 1 to 3 months. The high tight flag needs the double in 8 weeks or less.
questions.lesson_line: Same buy, same stop. The pole decides which card you are on.

wrong.High tight flag setup: 35% is nowhere near a double. The flag needs the near-double first.
wrong.A V off a crash low: Nothing here fell. It rose and tightened.

questions.q: Take it or pass?
questions.story: The stock fell 45% in two months. Then it doubled off the low in five weeks and now pauses near the high.
choices: Pass; a V off a crash
Take it; the pole doubled
Take it; the flag is tight
questions.answer: Pass; a V off a crash
questions.why: Pass. Not a V: in the 40 sessions before the pole began, the stock did not fall more than 30%. This one fell 45%. Bulkowski: avoid V shapes.
questions.lesson_line: A double off a crash is a repair, not a launch.

wrong.Take it; the pole doubled: The double is real, but it starts from a crash. That is the V the card rules out.
wrong.Take it; the flag is tight: A tight flag does not fix where the pole began.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought a stock that rose 291% in 34 sessions, then flagged six days. The breakout day traded a tenth of its average volume. Next morning it trades through your stop.
choices: Sell at the stop
Hold; the pole was huge
Widen the stop to the flag low
Buy more; it is cheaper
questions.why: Sell at the stop. After the entry, the stop is the exit. SRRK, December 2020: the biggest pole in the scan, and stopped the next session.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is an appointment, not a debate. Even after a perfect-looking pole.

wrong.Hold; the pole was huge: The size of the pole does not move the stop. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Widen the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up. Widening it is the mistake.
wrong.Buy more; it is cheaper: We never add, least of all to a trade going through its stop.

questions.q: The next morning it takes your stop. Was buying the gap a mistake?
questions.story: A 101% pole, then a nine-day flag 8.8% deep. The stock gaps open at 125.50 over the 121.91 buy point. You are filled. It closes at 121.75, the low of its day.
choices: No; a planned loss at the stop
Yes; never buy a gap
Yes; the stop was too tight
Yes; volume was too light
questions.answer: No; a planned loss at the stop
questions.why: No. A gap over the high inside the 4% line is bought at the open, and the stop is the exit. FSLR, August 2022: the next session's low, 118.13, took it.
questions.lesson_line: A loss at the stop is the cost of being there for the ones that work.

wrong.Yes; never buy a gap: A gap over the high is bought at the open when it is inside 4%. SOFI was, and ran.
wrong.Yes; the stop was too tight: The stop was the rule's stop, a few cents under the day's low.
wrong.Yes; volume was too light: It broke out on 1.47x volume. The close, not the volume, told the story.

questions.q: Was the loss a mistake?
questions.story: Bought at 175.81, stop 168.86. It reaches 2.35R, then falls back. On day 3 it trades through your stop.
choices: No; it never reached the 3R trim
Yes; you should sell at 2R
Yes; widen the stop next time
Yes; you should have added
questions.answer: No; it never reached the 3R trim
questions.why: No. The first trim is a third at 3R, and it never got there. The stop is the exit. Breakeven is allowed from 2R, ideally, which would make it a scratch.
questions.lesson_line: A trade that reaches 2R and comes back is still a planned loss, or a scratch.

wrong.Yes; you should sell at 2R: No rule sells at 2R. The hard rule is a third at 3R.
wrong.Yes; widen the stop next time: A wider stop is a bigger loss when it fails. The stop only moves up.
wrong.Yes; you should have added: We never add. The full size goes on at one price with one stop.

questions.q: What went wrong?
questions.story: A 101% pole, then a 15-day flag 8.5% deep. It breaks out on 1.48x volume, reaches 1.66R, then stalls. On day 7 it trades through your stop.
choices: Nothing; a valid flag failed
The stop should have been wider
You should have sold at 1R
The pole was too small
questions.why: Nothing. A valid flag that simply failed. IBD: these are high-risk bases, and many fail. The stop kept it to one R.
questions.lesson_line: Not every good setup works. The stop is what makes that fine.

wrong.The stop should have been wider: A wider stop only makes the same failure cost more.
wrong.You should have sold at 1R: No rule sells at 1R. The first trim is a third at 3R.
wrong.The pole was too small: The pole more than doubled. The setup was valid.

questions.q: Take the breakout or pass?
questions.story: A 123% pole, then a 16-day flag 17.2% deep. Volume in the flag runs 1.27x the pole's average.
choices: Pass; supply is coming in
Take it; the pole is huge
Take it at half size
questions.why: Pass. Flag volume ran 1.27x the pole's. Supply was coming in during the rest, not drying up. PDD, December 2020: best 0.0R, stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume in the flag is somebody selling. Wait for quiet.

wrong.Take it; the pole is huge: A huge pole does not cancel heavy selling in the flag.
wrong.Take it at half size: Rising flag volume ends the setup. It is not a size cue.

questions.q: High tight flag, or something else?
questions.story: A 99% pole, then a 24-day flag 12.7% deep on light volume. Five closes in the flag sit under the 21-day EMA.
choices: A flat base or a cup
A high tight flag
A bull flag
questions.answer: A flat base or a cup
questions.why: A flat base or a cup. Five flag closes sat under the 21-day EMA. A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup, not a high tight flag.
questions.lesson_line: A real flag rides its fast averages. Lose them and it is a different base.

wrong.A high tight flag: The flag should hold the 21-day EMA. Five closes under it fail that line.
wrong.A bull flag: Measure the pole: a bull flag follows a 20% to 30% run, not a near-double.

questions.q: Which grades higher on volume?
questions.story: Two flags after a double. Flag A trades 45% of the pole's average volume. Flag B trades 95% of it.
choices: Flag A
Flag B
The same; both pass
questions.why: Flag A. Flag volume at most 60% of the pole's is the A grade. CRNC's flag volume was barely under the pole's: a B on that line.
questions.lesson_line: Both pass the gate. The quieter flag earns the higher grade.

wrong.Flag B: Heavier flag volume is less drying up. It passes the gate but grades lower.
wrong.The same; both pass: Passing the gate is not the same grade. The card grades the lighter flag higher.

questions.q: Which context grades higher?
questions.story: Two stocks double in seven weeks. One runs on a news story with no earnings behind it. The other runs on a big earnings beat on heavy volume.
choices: The earnings beat
The news story
They grade the same
questions.why: The earnings beat. A real change behind the pole with heavy volume is the A+ context; a news-only story with no earnings is B-.
questions.lesson_line: Ask why it doubled. Earnings beat a headline.

wrong.The news story: A news-only story with no earnings is B- context on our card.
wrong.They grade the same: The pole's cause is a grade cue. A real change grades higher.

questions.q: Buy the break?
questions.story: A fast pole, then a flag of eight sessions, 18% deep. At the pattern high, price sits 11% above the 10-day average.
choices: Pass; too far over the 10-day
Buy; it is clearing the high
Buy with a wider stop
questions.why: Pass. Skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average, even at the pattern high.
questions.lesson_line: If the averages have not caught up, the flag is not done.

wrong.Buy; it is clearing the high: The trigger is real, but the stretch rule says skip it.
wrong.Buy with a wider stop: A wider stop does not fix a stretched entry.

questions.q: What about the last third?
questions.story: Two weeks after the breakout, the stock gaps up three days running on rising volume. You have already sold two thirds.
choices: Sell a big part into the burst
Hold; only the trail decides
Add; it is working
Move the stop to the flag low
questions.answer: Sell a big part into the burst
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long: sell a big part into it, a judgment call. These breakouts often go vertical.
questions.lesson_line: When it goes vertical, sell into the buyers. Do not wait for the trail.

wrong.Hold; only the trail decides: The trail still runs, but a climax burst is the time to sell into strength.
wrong.Add; it is working: We never add. The full size went on at one price.
wrong.Move the stop to the flag low: The stop only moves up, and the flag low is far below.

questions.q: What gets you out of the last third?
questions.story: Bought at 264.95, stop 255.06. You took a third at 3R and a third at 5R. It ran to about 354 and now turns down hard.
choices: A close below the trailing average
A trade under the flag low
A trade back to your 3R price
Nothing; hold for a double
questions.answer: A close below the trailing average
questions.why: A close below the trailing average. BIDU went to about 354 in three weeks, then collapsed under the flag low by late March. The trail gets you out first.
questions.lesson_line: These rockets come back as fast as they went up. The trail is your exit.

wrong.A trade under the flag low: By then most of the run is gone. BIDU fell under it by late March.
wrong.A trade back to your 3R price: That is not an exit rule. The last third rides the trail.
wrong.Nothing; hold for a double: Only 6% doubled in Bulkowski's study. Hoping is not a plan.

questions.q: An 85% success rate quoted on vendor sites is a win rate you can expect.
questions.why: False. It is 100 minus a 15% break-even failure rate on perfect trades with no stop. Our scan: 29.6% reached 3R before a fixed stop.
questions.lesson_line: Read a statistic before you trust it. Ask what it measured.

questions.q: A reader's mechanical scan of these found them a good short. What was Bonde's answer?
choices: Late flags fail; context decides
The scan is right; skip them all
Use a much wider stop on them
Buy the trendline break early
questions.why: Late flags fail; context decides. It cannot be traded as a mechanical system. Weigh the earnings and whether it is the first base.
questions.lesson_line: The pattern is the start. The context decides whether it is ours.

wrong.The scan is right; skip them all: Bonde did not drop the pattern. He said the reading becomes critical.
wrong.Use a much wider stop on them: He said nothing about the stop. His point was where the flag sits in the move.
wrong.Buy the trendline break early: Bulkowski found that entry fails too often. Bonde's answer was context.

questions.q: You are up 3.5R and a report lands in two days. Hold through it?
choices: No; hold only if up 5R
Yes; it is a winner
Yes, with a wider stop
Yes, if the flag was tight
questions.why: No. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R. At 3.5R you sell before it.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings are a coin flip on a gap. Only a 5R cushion rides through.

wrong.Yes; it is a winner: Being a winner is not enough. The line is 5R.
wrong.Yes, with a wider stop: A gap can jump any stop. The rule is about the cushion, not the stop.
wrong.Yes, if the flag was tight: The chart does not change the report rule.

questions.q: Buy it again?
questions.story: You were stopped out the day after a breakout. Two weeks later the stock builds a fresh tight flag and trades through its high.
choices: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
No; it already failed once
Yes, at double size
Yes, on the old stop
questions.answer: Yes, as a new trade, new stop
questions.why: Yes, as a new trade. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, with its own stop and every rule.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is not a ban. A new trigger is a new trade.

wrong.No; it already failed once: One stop-out does not end the stock. A new trigger is a new trade.
wrong.Yes, at double size: Size comes from the new stop and our risk, never from making it back.
wrong.Yes, on the old stop: A new trade gets its own stop, under the new day's low.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before a breakout. Count the pole. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; the pole doubled
Pass; the run is far too small
Pass; the flag is far too deep
questions.why: Take it. +129% in 14 sessions, then a 14-day sideways flag 15.0% deep that held the 21-day EMA. It ran to 10.9R.
questions.lesson_line: Count the pole first. A real double, then a quiet shelf: that is the setup.

wrong.Pass; the run is far too small: Look at the run in front of the shelf: well over a double, in weeks.
wrong.Pass; the flag is far too deep: The flag gave back 15.0% of price, a normal depth for this pattern.

questions.q: Hidden ticker, the day before it trades through a tight flag's high. Count the pole. Take it or pass?
choices: Pass; the pole never doubled
Take it; the flag is tight
Take it; it is a leader
questions.why: Pass. The pole was +78% in 40 sessions. A tight flag in a leader that never doubled is a bull flag, however tight. Best 1.88R, stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Tight is not enough. No double, no high tight flag.

wrong.Take it; the flag is tight: The flag is tight, and that is all. The pole decides the setup.
wrong.Take it; it is a leader: Leaders make bull flags too. The near-double is what this card needs.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On our card, the pole's rise takes ___ sessions or fewer.
questions.why: 40. Our card wants the rise done in 40 sessions, about 8 weeks. IBD describes a span of four to eight weeks.
questions.lesson_line: The pole is fast: 40 sessions or fewer, about 8 weeks.

questions.q: Which test does the pole fail?
questions.story: A leader rose 110% over 14 weeks, off a quiet base, after an earnings beat. Since then it has rested tight just under the high.
choices: The time test: too many weeks
The size test: too small a gain
The base test: not a quiet base
The cause test: no real change

wrong.The size test: too small a gain: A rise of 110% is a double and clears the size test.
wrong.The base test: not a quiet base: The story says it rose off a quiet base, so that test passes.
wrong.The cause test: no real change: An earnings beat is a real change, so that test passes.

questions.answer: The time test: too many weeks
questions.why: The time test. Our card wants the rise done in 40 sessions, about 8 weeks. 14 weeks is far past that, so it is no pole.
questions.lesson_line: A double over 14 weeks is not a pole. Speed is part of the pattern.

questions.q: On our card, the close is above the 50-day average at the trigger.
questions.why: True. Our card wants the close above the 50-day simple moving average at the trigger. It also wants the close above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: At the trigger, the close is above the 50-day and the 200-day.

questions.q: On our card, price is above a rising 10-day and a rising 21-day EMA at the trigger.
questions.why: True. The card wants price above both rising averages at the trigger. Kullamagi has the stock surf the rising 10- and 20-day through the consolidation.
questions.lesson_line: Price should ride rising fast averages into the trigger.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a ___, not a high tight flag.
questions.why: Cup. A base that lost the fast averages is a flat base or a cup, not a high tight flag. The flag must keep riding them.
questions.lesson_line: Lose the fast averages and it is a base, not a flag.

questions.q: Which tightness cue marks the A+ flag on our card?
choices: Closes that stay tight each week
Narrow daily ranges on every bar
The lowest volume seen in the pole
A gap up out of the flag

wrong.Narrow daily ranges on every bar: IBD's JDSU flag had wide weekly ranges and still had tight closes. Closes are the cue.
wrong.The lowest volume seen in the pole: Light volume grades the flag's volume. It is not the tightness cue.
wrong.A gap up out of the flag: A gap is a trigger event. It says nothing about tight closes inside the flag.

questions.answer: Closes that stay tight each week
questions.why: Tight weekly closes. IBD's JDSU flag had wild weekly ranges, but its closes were relatively tight. Our card calls tight weekly closes the A+ cue.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a flag by where it closes, not by its wicks.

questions.q: A high tight flag needs growing sales and earnings, or we skip it.
questions.why: False. Growing sales and earnings, or a real catalyst, are preferred but not required. The chart comes first.
questions.lesson_line: Preferred, not required. The chart comes first.

questions.q: What does our rule say?
questions.story: Every chart test is met: a double in seven weeks off a quiet base, a tight flag and a trigger. Sales growth stalled last quarter. A big new contract drove the pole.
choices: Keep it; the chart comes first
Pass; sales have to be growing
Wait until sales turn back up
Buy it, but only at half size

wrong.Pass; sales have to be growing: Growth is preferred, not required. A real catalyst counts, and the chart comes first.
wrong.Wait until sales turn back up: Waiting on sales is not a rule. The chart sets the entry.
wrong.Buy it, but only at half size: Size follows the grade and the stop, not a sales dip. The catalyst is real.

questions.answer: Keep it; the chart comes first
questions.why: Keep it; the chart comes first. Growing sales and earnings, or a real catalyst, are preferred but not required. Here a contract drove the pole.
questions.lesson_line: Growth is preferred, never required. The chart comes first.

questions.q: You buy at 100.00 and the flag low is 88.00. How far under your fill is a stop at the flag low, in percent?
questions.why: 12.0%. Our stops usually sit within about 3% of the buy. The flag low is far too wide, so it kills the idea but is not the stop.
questions.lesson_line: The flag low ends the idea. The stop is much closer.

questions.q: In Bulkowski's study, a stop a penny under the flag low meant taking an average 26% loss.
questions.why: True. That wide stop is why we do not use it. Ours is a few cents under the day's low; the flag low is the line that kills the idea.
questions.lesson_line: A flag-low stop is too far away. Ours is the day's low.
